newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan doomsday cult expected to avoid ban - sources.
newsitem.headline: Japan doomsday cult expected to avoid ban - sources.

text.p: Japan is likely to step back from invoking a never-before used law that could outlaw the doomsday cult accused of the 1995 Tokyo subway gas attack, judicial sources said on Tuesday.

The sources said a majority of the six members of a commission of jurists, academics and media figures, appointed by the justice minister to decide the future of the cult by the end of this month, were against banning it.

The commission has been debating for the past six months what action to take against Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect), which police have linked to the March 1995 subway attack in which 12 people died and 6,000 were made ill when sarin nerve gas was released on five trains.
"A majority of the commission members tend to believe that the group no longer poses a real threat," a commission source said.

To invoke a 1952 law on subversion, authorities have to testify to a court that a group has carried out indiscriminate acts of terrorism with a political motive and there is a likelihood of repeated attacks.
The Public Security Investigation Agency, an arm of the Justice Ministry, has demanded that the law be applied to the 10,000 member cult.
Since its enactment in 1952, the anti-subversion law has never been invoked, out of concern that it might violate human rights.

The commission sources said that in hearings they have held about the issue, subway victim groups and conservative politicians want a ban while civil liberties organisations and and cult members oppose the move.
Cult representatives have argued that the law violates constitutional freedoms of religion, speech and assembly.
If outlawed, members of the group would be banned from holding meetings, producing publications or conducting any business that could be construed as a group activity.
Even in the 1970s, when the Japan Red Army and other leftist groups were accused of bombings and assassinations, the law was not invoked.
All but two cult members directly accused of carrying out the subway attack have been arrested.
Many other members have left the sect, accusing cult guru Shoko Asahara of leading them astray.
Asahara is on trial on 17 charges connected with the subway attack, including murder and attempted murder.
